title: The best in the world is a local problem
content:
On a good day, my [bongo](http://www.puzzmo.com/play/bongo) score looks like this:

![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/seths.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Screenshot-2026-03-16-at-6.25.48-AM.jpg?resize=722%2C266&ssl=1)
Compared to all the people who have played this morning, it’s right at the top. That could be great…

Except I’m not being compared to every player in the world. The first graph is built to compare every player who has never previously won the competition.

![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/seths.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Screenshot-2026-03-16-at-6.25.56-AM.jpg?resize=716%2C306&ssl=1)
Here’s the curve of _all_ players, including the 500 previous champions. To win the day, you need to get through that dip that most players don’t achieve.

Same score, different ranking.

Here’s Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce running against the other parents at a school picnic:

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KkBwt8LRNqo)

I’m sure she deflated the egos of quite a few parents, the ones who usually win at these sorts of things.

Choosing our competition is the most productive decision we make each day.

The internet has made the world smaller, and the universe of competitors larger. But it’s still local–awareness, trust and convenience drive choice.

To be chosen, we need to be seen as the best in the world. But we get to choose which world.

title: This Is the Oldest Peace Treaty Ever Discovered
content:
The history of peace treaties goes back to around 1269 BCE, when Pharaoh Ramses II of Egypt and King Hattusilli III of the Hittite Empire put together what’s thought to be the first ever agreement between nations that hostilities should cease: in this case, over disputed Syrian territories. Over the last 120 years, archaeologists have unearthed fragments of this treaty in the ruined Hittite capital—and they just turned up another piece of the original.

Discovered in the rocky Büyükkale site in modern-day Türkiye, it contains articles 12 though 20 of the agreement and covers rules around how refugees should be treated, specifically stating that their homes shouldn’t be destroyed.

**Read more:**[**“Eating for Peace”**](https://nautil.us/eating-for-peace-237132)

The treaty came about after the epic Battle of Kadesh, a clash that involved thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of Egyptian and Hittite soldiers. While both sides claimed victory, it was effectively a bloody draw, and some 15 years later, the two sides decided to end their centuries-long conflict over Syrian and Mediterranean land.

Originally written on silver tablets that have been lost to time, the treaty has survived thanks to copies made on clay tablets and written in the cuneiform system: wedges cut into a surface that, like hieroglyphics, represent words, sounds, or syllables. The specific language used is that of the Akkadians, considered to be the first empire builders, who lived in Iraq between roughly 2400 BCE and 2200 BCE. (It would’ve made sense for the Egyptians and Hittites to use a third language that both sides could understand, and Akkadian was recognized as the international language of diplomacy in the Late Bronze Age.)

There’s a copper replica of the peace treaty on display at the United Nations headquarters in New York City, though, again, it hasn’t been recovered in its entirety. Researchers are hoping that further excavations at the Büyükkale site will uncover more fragments.

The copper replica of the treaty at the U.N. headquarters. _Credit: United Nations_

The overall themes of the accord cover friendship, peace, territorial boundaries, extradition, and mutual support. “We are united, and a bond of fraternity already exists among us and of peace, and it is better than the bond of fraternity and of peace that existed between the country of Egypt and the country of Hatti,” reads part of the agreement, as per a [translation](https://corum.ktb.gov.tr/EN-61494/kadesh-war-and-peace-treaty.html).

“This valuable discovery ... once again highlights Anatolia’s deep-rooted place in the history of peace and diplomacy,” Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, the Türkiye Minister of Culture and Tourism, posted on [social media](https://x.com/MehmetNuriErsoy/status/2101959686652149778). “This legacy, reaching from thousands of years ago to our present day, reminds us of our responsibility to protect human life and dignity.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Blood Cells From an 80-Year-Old Transformed into Young Brain Cells
content:
You started off as just two cells. Then those cells became four cells, which became eight cells, and so on. As you sit here reading this, your body has roughly 30-40 trillion cells, each performing one of hundreds of specialized jobs. Of course, on this differentiation journey there are points of no return. Once a cell is committed to a job, there’s no turning back—at least not without a little help.

Using a cocktail of transcription factors, scientists can reverse the differentiation process, transforming specialized cells back into pluripotent stem cells. These cells have the ability to become virtually any cell in the body. This method also immediately resets the cells’ epigenetic clocks, molecularly rejuvenating them in a way. Now, according to a new [study](http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/acel.70751) in _Aging Cell_, scientists have developed a way to skip this intermediate pluripotent stem cell step while keeping the youthful molecular profile.

**Read more: “**[**Do These Centenarians Hold the Key to Long Life in Their Blood?**](https://nautil.us/do-these-centenarians-hold-the-key-to-long-life-in-their-blood-1270732)**”**

A team of researchers led by neurobiologists from the University of Bonn in Germany successfully coaxed blood cell progenitors taken from an 80-year-old donor to become neural stem cells. According to the team, the resulting brain cells had an epigenetic age of under 20 years old. “We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells,” study author Oliver Brüstle said in a statement.

Because this new technique skips the pluripotent step, the rejuvenation of the cells occurs more gradually, allowing the researchers to track the process over a period of 100 days. “Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model,” Brüstle explained. “Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process.”

The team says getting a peek under the hood of how our brain cells age at the molecular level could shed light on age-related neural diseases. Or as Brüstle put it, “After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: I Seeded My Dreams and This Story Emerged
content:
Three years ago, I began a strange experiment—strange even for a poet. For nine months, I seeded my dreams with recorded poetry from Harvard University’s audio archive, then tried to capture the resulting dreams on the page. I called the project [Dreamfall](https://www.willdowd.net/dreamfall).

I relied on [Dormio](https://www.media.mit.edu/projects/sleep-creativity/overview/), a targeted dream incubation device from the MIT Media Lab. Worn like a glove, the device’s sensors tracked my descent into hypnagogia, the borderland between waking and sleep, where thoughts give way to hallucinatory imagery. As I crossed that threshold, Dormio played a prerecorded prompt (in this case, the crackling voice of a poet). Minutes later, it would sound a gong and begin recording, and I would groggily recount my dream before it could fade from memory.

**Read more:**[**“Faulty Memory Is A Feature, Not A Bug”**](https://nautil.us/faulty-memory-is-a-feature-not-a-bug-302075)

So why spend nine months falling asleep to the voices of dead poets? About twenty years ago, I developed a binocular vision disorder that makes it difficult to coordinate my eyes as they travel across a printed page. I was exiled from the immersive pleasure of reading. But dreaming seemed to offer a remarkably close analogue: imaginative flight while the body remains motionless, save for the eyes flicking from left to right. If I programmed my dreams with literature, could I find a back door into the lost world of books?

When I [spoke with _Nautilus_ in 2023](https://nautil.us/does-dream-inception-work-311117), I had no idea what my experiment would yield. _The Taste of Rain in Buenos Aires_, a collection of stories drawn from those dreams, is now out from Etruscan Press. One story, “A Sunset-Touch,” excerpted below, was seeded by a recording of Jorge Luis Borges lecturing at Harvard in 1967.

Borges became director of Argentina’s National Library just as his eyesight failed. Yet he continued to lecture extemporaneously around the world, drawing on the library he carried in his memory. He once described writing as “a guided dream.” More than a half century after his Harvard lectures, I fed his voice into Dormio and tested his claim.

The dream behind “A Sunset-Touch” came during a snowy New England winter—a season tailor-made for afternoon naps. In composing the story, I stayed faithful to its strange events but allowed myself freedom in the telling. Dream narratives do not unfold in sentences. Characters converse without speaking; whole backstories arrive in a flash of understanding; years pass in the space of an image. What feels self-evident in sleep would be bewildering on the page.

While writing “A Sunset-Touch,” I thought of myself as a dream journalist, responsible for reporting what I had witnessed, even when it made no sense. But fidelity was only part of my task. I tried to give the surreal experience enough connective tissue for readers to feel they had lived it—or dreamed it.

I hope Borges would approve.

Dream seed:

_Just when we’re safest, there’s a sunset-touch,_  
_A chorus-end from Euripides, somebody’s death._

—Robert Browning, “Bishop Blougram’s Apology” (as misquoted by Jorge Luis Borges, “The Riddle of Poetry”)

**A SUNSET-TOUCH**

I planned to sleep on the plane, but I’m seated next to an adorable little girl who won’t shut up.

She’s pestering her mother, who is sitting on her other side, with question after question.

“What’s that button do?”

“It turns on the reading light.”

The girl turns the reading light on and off, on and off.

“What’s that button do?” she chirps.

“It summons the flight attendant but don’t—”

Too late. The pressed button glows.

“What’s behind that door?” the girl asks. “The one with the red letters E-M-E-R-G-E-N-C-Y?”

“Don’t even think about it,” the mother snaps.

When an unsmiling flight attendant reaches us, I pretend to have pressed the button and order a Diet Coke.

_Thank you_, the mother mouths to me.

As I crack open my can and pour the fizzing soda into a tiny cup of ice, the girl voices further queries. She wants to know how many people are on board, which direction we’re flying, what country we’re above, and what the pilot’s middle name is.

Eventually, the mother inserts foam plugs into her ears and stops answering. Soon she is asleep.

The girl turns to me. “What keeps the plane in the air?”

“The engines,” I say.

“And what keeps the engines in the air?”

“The fuel.”

“And what keeps the fuel in the air?”

I can see I’ll soon be out of my depth. Fortunately, someone comes to the rescue. A man wearing large, owlish glasses peers over the seat in front of us. “I can tell you what keeps the plane in the air,” he announces.

“What?” says the girl.

With a twinkle in his magnified eyes, the man replies, “Angels.”

The girl looks suspiciously out of the oval window. “I don’t see one.”

“That’s because angels are invisible,” the man says.

The girl turns back to me. “Is he lying?” she demands.

Because I don’t want to get into a discussion about air pressure and fuel combustion, I back him up. “No, he’s not. Angels are real.”

“Have you ever seen one?” she asks, her brow furrowed.

“Well, no,” I admit.

“Then how do you know they’re real?”

“I spend a lot of time in libraries,” I say, “and sometimes, when I have a question and I can’t find the answer, you know what? The exact book I need turns up on my desk. Or falls off the shelf right at my feet. It’s not a coincidence. It’s the work of library angels. At least that’s what people call them.”

Seemingly satisfied with this explanation, the girl puts on headphones and starts watching the in-flight movie.

The man with the owl glasses is still twisted around in his seat. “So you believe in library angels?”

“Of course not,” I say, rattling the ice cubes in my cup.

He nods. “You’re right, obviously—they’re not _really_ angels. They’re the dead.”

I stop rattling my ice cubes.

He holds up a leathery hand. “Don’t get the wrong idea. These aren’t poltergeists knocking books off shelves at random. These are talented scholars we’re talking about. Devoted bibliophiles. Many apply, but only the most qualified are chosen. Believe me, it’s a highly coveted afterlife profession. Most of the departed are stuck doing hard labor.”

I decide to play along. “That seems a little unfair.”

“Not as unfair as you might think,” he says. “You’d be surprised how much work goes into the execution of librarial serendipities. These ‘library angels,’ as people call them, are each responsible for thousands of branches. You wouldn’t believe the time they spend on air travel alone.”

Now I furrow my brow. “But can’t the dead fly? Or, I don’t know, float?”

“Floating is impractical, and flying takes centuries to learn.”

“Angels can fly,” I point out. “Why don’t they just flit around from library to library, doing the work?”

The man with the owl glasses turns back around and reclines his seat. “I told you,” he says with a yawn. “The angels are too busy keeping planes in the air.”

We land and, after collecting my luggage, I check into a run-down hotel (the unemployment checks only go so far). The night is sweltering and the room is a furnace. I open the window, trying to tempt in a nonexistent breeze, and lie on the bed sweating.

I’ll never fall asleep in this heat. Plus, I’m nervous about my lecture in the morning. I was surprised they asked me, frankly, as I’ve never delivered a lecture in my life. I’m just another failed academic with a PhD and no job prospects. But the letter had my name right on it, as did the plane ticket included in the envelope. What will they think if I show up red-eyed and rumpled, not having slept a wink? I glance at the digital clock; its red digits wriggle like nightcrawlers in a jar.

The next morning, after downing three espressos at a corner café, I follow the map that came with my letter. I wind through a maze of slender, cobbled streets. Laundry flaps overhead. At last, I emerge onto a small square. Before me stands the headquarters of the International Borges Society.

The headquarters turns out to be located on the second floor of a dilapidated building, above a bar where a gang of septuagenarians are already drinking cervezas and playing chess. After an absurd pantomime with the bar’s owner, I’m led up a steep staircase and let inside.

The room has the chalky smell of a century-old schoolhouse. There are a few dozen chairs, a gap-toothed ceiling fan missing two blades, and a tilted lectern partially stabilized by a wedge of yellowed newspaper. I take my place behind the lectern and wait. Dust motes swirl in the liquid morning light.

When the society members arrive, I recognize them as the well-lubricated septuagenarians from downstairs. With a general popping of hip joints, they take their seats. The men rest their fedoras on their knobby knees, and I soon realize that waiting for silence would be folly—the coughing and spitting into handkerchiefs is ceaseless.

Since Borges always improvised his talks, it’s tradition that the annual lecturer—in this case, me—arrive blind to his topic. On top of the lectern lies a black felt bag. I reach into it, jostling a collection of wooden knickknacks inside. I draw one out. It’s a carved and painted tiger.

I clear my throat. “In the jungles of literature, the tiger has stalked…” I falter and start again. “For Borges, the tiger was a symbol…” My mind goes blank. “Tyger, tyger, burning in the night…” No, that’s not it. I swallow. I’m beginning to sweat in earnest now. Why did I ever accept this invitation?

Thankfully, an ambulance passes, its wailing siren buying me a few moments. I glance at the doorway, thinking maybe I could make a run for it. I notice that someone is lingering there, half in the room, half out. The owner of the gray flannel pant leg and the white canvas shoe must be waiting to hear the beginning of my lecture before committing to the full hour. I’m surprised the leg hasn’t withdrawn already.

When the siren fades into the distance, I close my eyes and begin again. “Let’s talk about stripes,” I say. “Not the stripes of tigers but of their prey. When a herd of zebras flees a beast red in tooth and claw, their black-and-white stripes create an optical illusion. The predator can’t tell where one zebra stops and another begins. He sees a single hide, one elongated animal loping across the savanna. Where’s the neck? he’s asking himself. Because of their stripes, the zebras are like a text without spaces between the words, and the tiger can’t read it. Yet if you mark one zebra with a red stripe, making it stand out from the rest, you’ve signed its death warrant. Humans are like zebras—most of us merge with the crowd, staying off the radar of the gods. But geniuses like Jorge Luis Borges are marked with a bright red stripe, and the gods can see them very clearly. And so the gods shower them with gifts—and pain.”

One of the society members falls asleep in his chair. A woman, possibly his wife, shakes him to no effect. The rest of my lecture is accompanied by the slumbering man’s heavy snores.

When it’s over, and I’ve shaken all the sweaty palms on offer, I stumble out into the dazzling sunlight, feeling relieved and thirstier than I’ve ever been in my life.

I take a long drink at a water fountain, letting the cool jet soak my face. When I pull back and shake my head like a dog, water droplets spray onto the gray flannel pant legs and the white canvas shoes of the man standing directly behind me. The man who was lingering in the doorway during my lecture. The man with the owl glasses.

He claps me on the shoulders. “You were good. A little rocky at the beginning, but once you got going—excellent stuff. Just what we’re looking for.”

I wipe my still-dripping face and wonder if I’m suffering heat stroke. “Why are you here? And who’s we?”

“Walk with me,” he says, hooking my arm and marching me down the street. “You should be honored, you know. We don’t make this offer very often. A new position opens every twenty, maybe thirty, years.”

He steers me to the left and we pass under a stone proscenium. “In this age of _algorithms_”—his face screws up in disgust at the word—“some consider our work redundant, but you and I know better.”

He leads me past a cage of spider monkeys who jeer at us through the bars. “The position is unpaid, of course,” he says. “But the job is its own reward.”

We hurry by a large paddock. Quizzical-looking llamas raise their heads to stare at us. “What job?” I demand.

An elephant trumpets in the distance. “You know the answer to that question,” he says.

After a few paces, I come to a dead stop. “Library angel,” I breathe.

The man nods. “There’s a catch, though I’m sure you’ve guessed already.”

“I’d have to be dead, wouldn’t I?” I say quietly.

“Yes,” he says with a smile. “You’ll have to cross over, I’m afraid. But it’s a small price to pay.”

I feel dazed. I tug my arm free and steady myself against a nearby stone ledge.

The man polishes his glasses on his sleeve. “So, what do you say?” he asks. “Do you accept?”

I lean against the ledge, feeling the warmth baked into the stone by the morning sun. The day is already oppressively hot. My suit is damp with sweat and itchy around the collar. I think of a library, how delicious its dim, chilled air would be right now. And I imagine the relief of finally, at long last, being gainfully employed.

“I accept,” I say.

With one stroke, the man paints a red stripe across my chest. Then he shoves me backward, over the ledge and into the tiger enclosure. ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Is ‘Attention’ the Essence of Intelligence?
content:
![Image 1: Qualia: Essays that go where curiosity leads](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2050/01/QUALIA-Banner-WITH-SPACER-1-1720x223.webp)

E verything that’s swept the world since the 2022 release of ChatGPT — “the AI economy”; data centers; chatbots acting as best friends, doctors, and mathematicians; talk of existential risk — it all starts, in some sense, with an intern in a University of Montreal lab named Dzmitry Bahdanau.

It was 2014. The 23-year-old Belarusian, who had been coding competitively since he was a kid but hadn’t done academic research before, was asked to help figure out how to get a computer to translate sentences from English to French. Bahdanau was working with artificial neural networks, which had already shown promise in pattern-recognition tasks such as deciphering handwriting and identifying objects in photos. The networks learn to recognize patterns by strengthening and weakening connections between nodes in response to training data. Bahdanau quietly doubted their potential to achieve anything like human-level intelligence, but his adviser, the computer scientist Yoshua Bengio, and the postdoc on the project, Kyunghyun Cho, were believers. And translation was widely seen as a formidable and interesting problem for neural networks to try to solve.

Translation is not as simple as swapping each English word for a French one. Languages have different grammatical structures and are riddled with idioms and connotations, all of which had long stymied attempts to automate the process. You can’t simply implement rules of translation because there are none. But neural networks seemed promising because they learn by example. They can be trained on huge databases of paired English and French sentences to, eventually, absorb the quasi-rules, exceptions, and subtleties.

Results had been mediocre, though; the longer the sentence, the worse neural networks performed. That’s because researchers were trying to cram each sentence’s data into a fixed amount of memory before decoding the sentence in the target language. It was a bottleneck that limited how complex and sophisticated translations could be. The network architecture just wasn’t right.

So Bahdanau tried something different. “It was just obviously the right thing to do — one of these things that happens once in a while in science where it’s just very clear to someone who is not very experienced in the field,” he recalled, speaking to me from Montreal, where he still works in AI. “And it just worked. From the very first attempt.”

Bahdanau’s trick, a mathematical operation that he, Cho, and Bengio referred to as “attention,” [enabled their neural network to translate long sentences (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) just as well as short ones. That meant the approach was scalable. Other AI researchers at the time quickly integrated attention into their neural network designs. Then, in 2017, a team at Google devised a new kind of neural network architecture called a transformer that supercharged the attention method and stripped away everything else. The team’s paper, “[Attention Is All You Need (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762),” reported that transformers achieved state-of-the-art translation while requiring a fraction of the computation needed to train prior models. The paper, which has since been cited more than 250,000 times, was a watershed moment in AI. Large language models such as ChatGPT and Claude followed.

Given the staggering power that’s been unleashed, it’s worth asking what this attention mechanism _is_ exactly, why it is “all you need,” and why machine translation was the task that unlocked it all. Attention is a way for us to understand how a single AI model can converse with us, diagnose diseases, generate realistic videos, [solve long-standing math problems](https://www.quantamagazine.org/ai-has-solved-one-of-maths-1-million-millennium-prize-problems-20260908/), and more. Is it somehow at the heart of intelligence — artificial and otherwise?

![Image 2](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/QUALIA-Separator-2.webp)

Sentences with pronouns such as “it” in them illustrate the challenge that attention overcomes. Consider: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” And: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too wide.” To translate these sentences correctly into French, an AI model must determine that, in the first one, “it” refers to the animal, which is a masculine word in French, so the translation should use that form of the pronoun, _il_. But in the second sentence, “it” refers to the street, a feminine word that requires a different pronoun, _elle_. How can the machine figure this out?

Bahdanau remembered doing translation exercises when he was learning English in school. To write each next word of his translated sentence, he’d have to glance all around the source text to figure out what should come next. “Literally you have your source sentence on the left and your writing on the right, and you’ll be, like, turning your head, left-right, left-right,” he said. “That process is what I expressed as a neural mechanism.” The tool of attention that he gave to his neural network was a mathematical way for the network to identify the word or words anywhere in a sentence that would most inform the next word of the translation. In the case of our ambiguous pronoun, “it,” the system navigates the rest of the sentence to determine which words affect its meaning the most.

A transformer consists of many layers of nodes connected to nodes in adjacent layers. When a sentence is fed into a transformer, each word is first converted into a numerical representation called a vector, which we can imagine as an arrow pointing in a certain direction. These vectors pass through the network, and numbers called weights (determined by the model’s training) dictate how they are transformed in each layer. The weights turn each word’s current vector representation into three new vectors specific to that word — a “query,” “key,” and “value” — that each serve a different purpose in the attention operation.

The network performs this operation several times in parallel through systems called attention heads. An attention head compares each word’s query with the keys of all the other words in the sentence. How well these vectors match up — how much they point in the same direction — determines how strongly the value of each other word contributes to a new, updated vector for the word at hand. Information about other words in the sentence literally becomes incorporated into each word’s representation. The system is converting context into math.

When “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired” enters a transformer, the first stack of layers in the network, known as the encoder, uses the attention operation to build up a contextual understanding of the sentence. In each layer, each attention head generates a query (along with a key and value) for “it.” This query vector can be thought of as a request for information that exists elsewhere in the sentence. For instance, in a deep layer (after the network has already accumulated information about words), the query for “it” might be interpretable as: “I need an earlier noun that could plausibly be the thing that is tired.” Meanwhile, the key associated with “animal” might effectively advertise itself as a noun that’s capable of being tired, among many other features. Its key therefore matches the query better than the key for “street.” And that causes the value associated with “animal” to contribute more heavily to the updated representation of “it.”

That new, context-enriched representation of “it” passes into the next layer. There, the network performs attention all over again. Successive rounds give the words increasingly rich representations of themselves.

Experts say it’s often hard to interpret what any given attention head is doing, but collectively they pick up on many kinds of relationships, from the partnership between nouns and verbs to the association between living beings and feelings. Later layers build on associations established by earlier layers, so that by the time the sentence emerges from the encoder, “it” is imbued with something resembling meaning.

After that, the second part of the transformer, the decoder, produces the French translation one word at a time, using attention to draw on the encoder’s numerical representations of the English words as it decides which French word to spit out next. The contextual information encoded in the English sentence helps translate “it” as the masculine _il_.

Crucially, no one had to tell a transformer that animals get tired and streets may be wide. The neural network discovers such associations during training, by learning from huge numbers of English sentences paired with their French translations. These associations get built into the weights. The network starts out with random weights that produce unhelpful queries, keys, and values, and thus poor translations. But each translation error sends a correction signal backward through the network that slightly alters the weights that produced it. Through trillions of these adjustments, the network eventually generates useful vectors that yield correct translations, even when it processes sentences it has never seen before.

Attention turned out to be the right mathematical operation for linking words and building context — the fundamentals of translation. And when you can translate blocks of text of unlimited size, it seems you can do anything.

![Image 3](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/QUALIA-Separator-2.webp)

A neural network that has learned enough about language to translate sentences from English into French can also complete sentences in either language. Predicting the next word of a translation is, in other words, a subtask of the more general task of “predicting the next word,” period. And that’s what large language models do. They’re trained on the contents of the entire internet, learning which words should attend to which other words in all sorts of contexts. They process and reprocess the whole dataset and try trillions of times to predict the next word in whatever part of the web they happen to be in at any point during training. The connections between neurons in these models are gradually tweaked in a way that produces patterns of attention between words that are ever more useful for predicting the next word in any context — or for producing an appropriate response to a prompt from a human.

From the ability to translate the word “it,” we somehow got a revolution.

“That’s quite a leap, isn’t it?” said Llion Jones, one of the authors of “Attention Is All You Need,” who is now the chief technology officer of Sakana AI.

Jones and others suspect that predicting the next word, which is known as language modeling, is “AI-complete”: a task so difficult that solving it means you have arguably solved AI in general. The reason it may be AI-complete is that this task includes, as a subtask, virtually anything humans do in written form. “The internet has translations,” Jones notes. “So if I said ‘“The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired” in French is [blank],’ then in order to complete that sentence, the transformer needs to be able to translate into French. If I say ‘2 + 3 is [blank],’ it needs to do arithmetic. If it sees a bunch of mathematical symbols in a row and wants to know what comes next, it needs to understand high-level mathematics. If I say ‘The president of the United States is [blank],’ it needs to know facts. So being able to predict the next word requires you to be able to do all these things. And because it’s AI-complete, language modeling is kind of the closest definition that we have to intelligence.”

It might not be apt to say that an LLM “knows” or “understands” anything — not in the way that a human does — but that’s just how we’re accustomed to talking about the abilities they display. Regardless, attention is the tool by which artificial neural networks access and convey meaning, association, and context, often well enough to astonish us with their fluency. (For tasks such as advanced mathematics, today’s frontier AI models often have more explicit formal reasoning and proof verification systems layered on top of their language modeling to check their work.)

But what about human intelligence? Might our brains employ a mechanism similar to the mathematical operation Bahdanau invented? After all, we, too, do something akin to “producing the best possible next word” when we speak, write, and even think. Perhaps our form of intelligence is tantamount to language modeling, too?

Cognitive scientists have begun to study this question — a new version of the ancient question of how language relates to thought. To be sure, the success of LLMs shows how much information about the world is encoded in the statistical patterns of language alone. The question is: When we master language, does intelligence come for free?

[Recent research (opens a new tab)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07522-w) persuades me that human thought is not purely linguistic (and most other animals’ intelligence is not linguistic at all): When we are thinking, more brain regions light up than just the specialized networks in the cerebral cortex that are associated with language. Language is how we _communicate_ about the world, but our thoughts seem to draw on sensory impressions, physical and social experiences, memories, and reasoning abilities that exist at least partly [outside the brain’s language networks](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-polyglot-neuroscientist-resolving-how-the-brain-parses-language-20251205/). So language modeling seems to be merely a powerful component of human cognition, not its equivalent or source.

As for how _we_ do “it” — how I instantly understand that it’s the animal rather than the street that is tired — no one yet knows. Jones, for his part, now thinks that attention is _not_ all you need to truly master language modeling. After all, the brain evidently accomplishes this task far more efficiently than transformers do. We converse fluently without having read the whole internet even once, and without burning as much energy. “The current paradigm won’t solve this [efficiency] problem,” Jones said. “You seem to have to jump to something very, very different.”

Regardless of what our own neural mechanisms might be, it makes sense to me in hindsight that solving translation unlocked AI. Whether you’re human or machine, the ability to translate effectively means you have understood, in some sense. Now the machines understand so much — effectively, at least — that we hardly know what to think anymore.

# James Baldwin on How Love (Finally) Finds You

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: James Baldwin on How Love (Finally) Finds You](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/baldwin_boggs.jpg?fit=320%2C434&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Baldwin-Love-Story-Nicholas-Boggs/dp/125043775X/?tag=braipick-20)

Our language betrays our self-betrayals: We speak of finding love, as if it were an undiscovered eighth continent or a habitable world in another solar system, as if it got lost like the Little Red Riding Hood or the names of the women who painted the caves. [Like the paradoxical notion of finding yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/06/07/robert-penn-warren-democracy-poetry-finding-yourself/), the notion of finding love pulsates with equal parts helplessness and hubris — a rueful recognition that something is missing from your life and a belief that it falls on you to do the looking, that if you only look hard enough and long enough, you will achieve the goal of finding it. But no one, not one person in the history of the heart, achieved love by striving.

From the vantage of love, it is you who are lost; it is love that finds you — and [not the way you expected](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/08/14/how-love-comes-to-you/).

No one has articulated this more perfectly, more poignantly, than [James Baldwin](https://themarginalian.org/tag/james-baldwin) (August 2, 1924–December 1, 1987) in a conversation with his young filmmaker friend Sedat Pakay, quoted in Nicholas Boggs’s altogether excellent biography [**_Baldwin: A Love Story_**](https://www.amazon.com/Baldwin-Love-Story-Nicholas-Boggs/dp/125043775X/?tag=braipick-20) (which also gave us the [moving letter](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/08/26/james-baldwin-orilla-bill-miller/) Baldwin received at the peak of his fame and his heartbreak from his childhood teacher).

![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/baldwin_typewriter.jpg?resize=680%2C326&ssl=1)

James Baldwin at work

Having turned his entire life around to follow his improbable Turkish lover to Istanbul, Baldwin reflects:

> I will never be able to deny for any reason at all is a certain power that I had to deal with, which has dealt with me, which is called _love._ And love comes in very strange packages. And I think everything depends in life on whether or not you are able to accept what comes to you. Because it never comes to you the way you think it will. It never comes to you the way you’re taught it will. It comes as it comes.

Never having imagined that love would make of the Harlem River an estuary to the Bosphorus, Baldwin finds himself reckoning with the broader meaning of it all:

> Love takes off the masks that we fear we cannot live without and know we cannot live within. I use the word “love” here not merely in the personal sense but as a state of being, or a state of grace — not in the infantile American sense of being made happy but in the tough and universal sense of quest and daring and growth.

The trouble, of course, is that we can choose, without knowing we are choosing, to stay behind the mask, chose being sure over being seen, chose control — which is always the feeling of control, never the fact of control — over possibility. The notion of finding love suffers the same pitfall, for it presumes that the searcher is in control of the find. [Elsewhere](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/06/06/james-baldwin-giovannis-room-love-choice/), Baldwin razes through the delusion:

> People who believe that they are strong-willed and the masters of their destiny can only continue to believe this by becoming specialists in self-deception. Their decisions are not really decisions at all — a real decision makes one humble, one knows that it is at the mercy of more things than can be named — but elaborate systems of evasion, of illusion, designed to make themselves and the world appear to be what they and the world are not.

Ultimately, love asks of us the same thing life does — to meet it on its terms. Baldwin writes:

> People can’t, unhappily, invent their mooring posts, their lovers and their friends, anymore than they can invent their parents. Life gives these and also takes them away and the great difficulty is to [say Yes to life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/10/01/yes/).
