title: The Madman Who Saved Mothers: The Invention of Handwashing and the Bittersweet True Love Story Behind ‘Frankenstein’
content:
**_This essay is adapted from [\_Traversal\_](https://www.themarginalian.org/traversal/)._**

[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/traversal_cover.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/traversal/)“Death may snatch me from you, before you can weigh my advice,” [Mary Wollstonecraft](https://themarginalian.org/mary-wollstonecraft) wrote in the philosophical novel she wouldn’t live to finish, addressing a daughter she was yet to have. “Always appear what you are, and you will not pass through existence without enjoying its genuine blessings, love and respect.”

In late 1791, as important men were sitting down in America to make ten amendments to the young country’s constitution, which they called a Universal Bill of Rights, Wollstonecraft was sitting down in England to complete _A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: with Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects_ — the beacon of political philosophy, inspired by Paine’s treatise, that would expand the universal to include all chromosomal arrangements, “demanding justice for one half of the human race” and laying the foundation of women’s political power, not by shaming and blaming the oppressor but by painting a passionate portrait of possibility.

When Wollstonecraft’s publisher invited her to a dinner celebrating one of those important men — Thomas Paine, whose landmark insistence on the right of the people to overthrow their rulers had inspired Wollstonecraft’s treatise — another of the publisher’s most successful and controversial authors was also there: the radical political philosopher [William Godwin](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/01/30/william-godwin-enquirer-education/).

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/godwin_wollstonecraft.jpg?resize=680%2C415&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/traversal/)

William Godwin (portrait by James Northcote) and Mary Wollstonecraft (portrait by John Opie)

Both Wollstonecraft and Godwin, who had never before met, had made their reputations on the bold denunciation of institutions, including the institution of marriage: Wollstonecraft in her _Vindication_ and Godwin in _An Enquiry Concerning the Nature of Political Justice_, which issued a rigorously reasoned eight-book call for a society of equals, indicting government, religion, and marriage as oppressive forces that limit individual freedom and gape the abyss of inequality. Government and religion, Godwin argued, would be rendered obsolete with sufficient advancement of human knowledge and morality. “Marriage, as now understood,” he wrote, “is a monopoly, and the worst of monopolies. So long as two human beings are forbidden, by positive institution, to follow the dictates of their own mind, prejudice will be alive and vigorous.”

Wollstonecraft inveighed against marriage as the only means for women to “rise in the world,” which in turn reduced their aspirations to those of “mere animals” and made them act as children once they did enter this institution of wholesale dependency. What she called for instead — equal access to education and an emphasis on the intellectual and moral development of girls, rather than their looks, dress, and manners — seems banal by our present standards, almost embarrassing. The luxury of being embarrassed by it — in just five human lifetimes, in a species 7,500 generations old — is the measure of our progress.

She had seen firsthand the moral, emotional, and bodily tyranny of an institution that considered the wife property of the husband, a creature owed as much sympathy and tenderness as a boot. As a child growing up in a house shaken by the cries of her own mother, regularly raped and beaten by her alcoholic husband, Wollstonecraft had stood sentinel before her mother’s door to keep her father from entering, which only aggravated his brutality. In a culture where just four women successfully obtained a divorce in the whole of a century, she came to see that to salvage the family, one had to revise the entire political foundations of society.

When the two philosophers met at their publishers’ dinner, the balding and reserved Godwin — a man so afraid of emotion that he never cared for music — found Wollstonecraft — a woman of symphonic intellect and unselfconscious passions — too eager to dominate the conversation with Paine. The middle child in a brood of thirteen, Godwin had always been introverted, awkward, and greatly challenged at attuning to the emotional states and needs of others. He regarded his peculiarity with both self-awareness and genuine bafflement:

> I have a singular want of foresight on some occasions as to the effect what I shall say will have on the person to whom it is addressed. I therefore often appear rude, though no man can be freer from rudeness of intention and often get a character for harshness that my heart disowns.

Wollstonecraft was extroverted, her quick mind coupled with a kind of social magnetism, but the very capacity for large thought and feeling that made her so magnetic also made her capable of despair so fathomless that she came to regard herself as “a strange compound of weakness and resolution,” marked by a great “defect” of mind and a “wayward heart” that creates its own misery.

For the two philosophers, love did not barge through the barn door of animal passion — it entered slowly, quietly, through the sun porch of shared ideals and mutual respect. Respect begot friendship begot love. Wollstonecraft came to see the “tender affectionate creature” from which Godwin’s coolly reasoned idealism sprang — his pursuit of political justice was at bottom a philosophy of universal sympathies and unconditional kindness, impulses of which his own nature was woven. Godwin discovered above the gratifications of being admired the gladness of being seen:

> After all one’s philosophy it must be confessed that the knowledge that there is some one that takes an interest in one’s happiness, something like that which each man feels for his own, is extremely gratifying.

There is something singularly endearing in his matter-of-fact account of how their relationship developed:

> The partiality we conceived for each other was in that mode which I have always considered as the purest and most refined kind of love. It grew with equal advances in the minds of each… When in the course of things the disclosure came there was nothing in the matter for either party to disclose to the other. There was no period of throes and resolute explanations attendant upon the tale. It was friendship melting into love.

In his autobiography, never published in his lifetime, he would eventually acknowledge that “there is nothing that the human heart more irresistibly seeks than an object to which to attach itself.” When he did attach himself to Wollstonecraft, it was a molecular bond that staggered him, altered him.

In the first days of spring in 1797, in the small churchyard of St. Pancras, four months into her pregnancy, Mary and William entered a trailblazing marriage of equals, then took up residence together in a home where they shared a bed and a value system but kept separate studies, Wollstonecraft writing and receiving visitors in a room of her own, and Godwin in his. The choice to marry against their stated credos had puzzled both their public admirers and their private circle. It mattered little, even the response from Godwin’s mother, spiked with the fine quills of passive aggression of which only mothers are capable: “Your broken resolution in regard to matrimony encourages me to hope that you will ere long embrace the Gospel.”

Convinced that their child was to be a boy, the parents-to-be named him William. Wollstonecraft resumed work on a book of moral lessons for children, which William Blake would later illustrate. Godwin channeled their daily conversations about how to bring up happy, intelligent, and morally elevated children in a series of essays later published as [_The Enquirer_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/01/30/william-godwin-enquirer-education/) his most timeless, if least known, book: an incisive inquiry into how we become who we are, laying out a radical new vision for optimal parenting and early childhood education.

“William” arrived on August 30, 1797, and was corrected, without fret or fanfare, to a Mary. After nine hours of labor and a difficult birth, the placenta and fetal membranes failed to leave Wollstonecraft’s uterus. A surgeon was summoned to extract it, rushing in from the street to plunge his hands into her flesh.

Within hours, the young mother was shivering with a savage fever.

* * *

Exactly fifty summers later, the Vienna General Hospital — one of the best teaching hospitals in the world — found itself the epicenter of a menacing medical mystery blackening the crucible of life with death: Young women were dying in agony by the legion shortly after giving birth.

The hospital had two maternity wards — one staffed by elite obstetricians and their medical students, the other by midwives with no formal medical training. (This was an era when [the world’s university doors were closed to women](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/27/lise-meitner/).) Tenfold more mothers were dying of puerperal fever in the first.

The medical elders initially assumed that the students were treating the pregnant women too roughly. But retraining didn’t change the ratio. Baffled, these thoroughly trained scientists fell to superstition — a priest walked through the doctors’ ward ringing a bell for each death and a theory emerged that the haunting sound was terrifying the living mothers into dying.

A young Hungarian doctor by the name of Ignaz Semmelweis, in his first year as assistant professor at the hospital, [wrote in his diary](https://www.amazon.com/Doctors-Plague-Childbed-Semmelweis-Discoveries/dp/0393052990/?tag=braipick-20):

> Even to me myself it had a strange effect upon my nerves when I heard the bell hurried past my door; a sigh would escape my heart for the victim that once more was claimed by an unknown power. The bell was a painful exhortation to me to search for this unknown cause with all of my might.

![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/IgnazSemmelweis_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C716&ssl=1)

Ignaz Semmelweis

When the pastor was asked to stop making his bell rounds, the deaths continued and the sigh kept bellowing in the young doctor’s heart as he bent his mind around the mystery. He catalogued all the visible variables and pored over the data, but it told no discernible story. Because the unknown will always be greater than the sum of all our analyzable knowns, because the sum is always [“simpler than its parts,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/04/24/muriel-rukeyser-willard-gibbs/) the history of science, the history of knowledge, is a rosary of breakthroughs that arrive through the side door of our reasoned theories. One day, Semmelweis’s mentor was teaching dissection at the morgue when a student accidentally nicked the professor’s finger with the scalpel while cutting open the cadaver on the table. Within days, he died a horrific death. A familiar death. It devastated Semmelweis, but it also pressed his face against the revelation — the doctors and medical students at the hospital were doing the exact same thing with the pregnant women: dissecting cadavers at the morgue, which none of the midwives did, and immediately going into the maternity ward to touch open flesh.

The young doctor realized that the men’s hands transferred some particle of death to the vulnerable living. He called them “cadaver particles” and set about devising ways to eradicate them, experimenting with various washing solutions and testing his results by smell alone — did his hands still have the putrid cadaver smell after washing them in the different agents. Eventually, he settled on a solution of chlorine and lime — bleach not strong enough to burn his hands, but strong enough to vanquish the other and, with it, the cadaver particles he theorized. When he implemented the protocol at his ward, the death count plummeted to that of the other ward.

![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/handwashing_marginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C566&ssl=1)

That year, Louis Pasteur began his crystallography research that would lead to the birth of germ theory more than a decade later. The notion that some invisible unit of matter could unravel a body was still inconceivable. Semmelweis was a brilliant theorist and a fine empiricist, but a terrible communicator. He took the opposite of Mary Wollstonecraft’s approach, pouring polemics into letters to every major hospital and medical school, pummeling colleagues with that least effective of all behavioral change strategies: shaming. He went as far as calling doctors who didn’t wash their hands murderers and warned medical students that unless they adopted his protocol, they would be accomplices in an epochal crime.

Unsurprisingly, Semmelweis was largely dismissed; unsurprisingly, he grew increasingly cantankerous. By the time he was in his early forties, the idealistic young doctor had undergone a staggering physiological and psychological change — he looked at least sixty, had frequent detonations of temper, and suffered baffling lapses of memory in the midst of lectures. The mysterious malady — possibly early-onset Alzheimers, possibly tertiary syphilis, likely some parallel discomposure of body and spirit — made him unbearable to be around.

One day, a colleague lured him to an asylum on the pretext of seeing a new facility. When Semmelweis realized he was about to be committed against his will, he raged to get away, but was brutalized by the wardens and put into a straitjacket.

He died two weeks later from an infection contracted from the beating.

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/HaemolyticStreptococcus_Marginalian.jpg?resize=611%2C600&ssl=1)

_Haemolytic streptococcus_

Four years later, two French scientists discovered the _microbes en chainettes_ — “microbe chains” — of his hypothesized “cadaver particles,” which Pasteur would identify as the bacterium _haemolytic streptococcus_ a decade later. It was ultimately a nurse — Florence Nightingale — whose [extraordinary data diagrams](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/05/22/florence-nightingale-flowers/) and passionate advocacy persuaded the medical establishment to standardize hospital sanitization.

* * *

Just before eight on a late-summer morning ten days after giving birth, Mary Wollstonecraft drew her last breath, leaving behind a fragile baby girl, a baffled philosopher stony with heartache, and an angel-winged William Blake etching.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/blake_maryshelley.jpg?resize=552%2C696&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/23/william-blake-mary-wollstonecraft/)

[_The Child Mary Shelley (at her Mother’s Death)_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/23/william-blake-mary-wollstonecraft/) by William Blake

For Godwin, who had spent his life sieging religion with the artillery of reason, the loss was total and irrevocable. The notions of personal immortality and reunion with loved ones in an imaginary afterlife were the pacifier of puerile minds. And yet loss unlatches an emotional trapdoor beneath our firmest cerebral convictions, plunging us into elemental questions that live beyond our reasoned beliefs, childlike in their disbelieving sincerity. It was such a question that sprang unbidden to my atheist engineer grandmother’s lips as she stood over the hospital bed holding the dead body of my atheist engineer grandfather, her love of half a century: _Where did you go, my darling?_

The guarded Godwin kept a diary more like a ship’s log than a discursive journal of an inner life:

“Seneca, Ep. 8, 9.”

“Call from Coleridge.”

“Queen dies.”

On the day of his beloved’s death, this man of factual records could not bring himself to name the fact. All he wrote in the ledger was “20 minutes before 8,” followed by an interminable sequence of dashes suturing the unspeakable.

“– — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — ”

By evening, he was able to write to his oldest friend with a confused fusion of dissociation and disconsolation:

> My wife is now dead. She died this morning at eight o’clock… I firmly believe that there does not exist her equal in the world. I know from experience we were formed to make each other happy. I have not the least expectation that I can now ever know happiness again. When you come to town, look at me, talk to me, but do not — if you can help it — exhort me, or console me.

In the corner, his baby daughter was sleeping in her crib. She would learn to read by tracing the letters on her her mother’s tombstone and would come to write, while still a teenager, an epochal reckoning with the eternal interplay of life and death.

The year her _Frankenstein_ was published, Ignaz Semmelweis was born in a Hungarian hospital.

title: We Are Already Post-Human
content:
Credits

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

From Silicon Valley to the Vatican, across kitchen tables and in the halls of power, the world is astir over the question of whether humans will be able to control the AIs we’ve created. But that begs the question: What does it mean to be “human”?

One place to start sorting this all out is what Confucian philosophy calls “rectification” — naming things for what they actually are.

To N. Katherine Hayles, author of “Bacteria to AI: Human Futures with our Non-human Symbionts,” we are already “post-human.”

As she explained to Claire Webb in a recent Futurology [podcast](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rryjPdKMxO4), the concept of “human” is culturally and historically contingent. These days, she says, there is still the dominant view that arose with the Enlightenment of the human as an autonomous, singular entity with “rational free will.”

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rryjPdKMxO4)

For Hayles, that has never been true because humans have never existed as an entity apart but have always been “woven in the web” of a surrounding environment, or “Umwelt.” It is the symbiotic interactions within that interdependence which determine the signs we sense, the meaningful interpretation of the information we process, the decisions we make, and the actions we take that define who we are.

The most obvious example of our relational interdependence with non-human life is the gut bacteria within us, the biological functions of which we’d perish without.

The false notion of self-enclosed human autonomy is even less true today, she argues, because “we are already in a deeply symbiotic relationship with computational media — chips, routers, devices, microwaves, etc. They have become the controllers, processors and disseminators of a flow of information” in which we are inextricably enmeshed — and, in advanced societies, without which we couldn’t survive. If it all crashed, we couldn’t transport food, fly airplanes or operate the stock market. We’d quite literally live in the dark.

As Hayles describes it, this condition amounts to “distributed cognition and distributed decision-making” between human and non-human participants. She calls these “cognitive assemblages” or “networked intelligence.”

In short, we are “post-human” because we are inseparably joined in an “integrated cognitive framework” with computational media.

## **Close To Singularity**

This post-human condition would seem to place us some distance along the continuum toward Singularity, the full fusion of humans and intelligent machines. By definition, this symbiosis blurs the line of who or what is in control.

In a related Futurology podcast, Kevin Kelly [tells](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dqr82eem4Zw) Nils Gilman that “we are already in the Singularity.” From his northern California perch, Kelly has been surfing the waves of technological innovation and cultural transformation for decades, going back to his time as co-founder of The Whole Earth Catalog with Stewart Brand and then Wired magazine.

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dqr82eem4Zw)

What Kelly means by “already in” is that human/machine fusion is a presently ongoing process that doesn’t suddenly cross some rapturous threshold, but incrementally unfolds with the accelerated deepening of the “integrated cognitive framework” Hayles talks about.

We can’t clearly see the massive change taking place now in its pixelated form, but will only be able to recognize the fuller picture of what has taken place from a future retrospective standpoint. Our perspective is clouded, says Kelly, by the fact that “we are living inside the event horizon.”

For Kelly, the Singularity is not a closed process with a fixed endpoint, but perpetually open to the emergence of new creative forms and unexpected symbiotic combinations, what the complexity scientist Stuart Kauffman calls the “adjacent possible” that can’t be foretold. “The Singularity is always near,” as Kelly puts it, but forever remains on the elusive horizon.

## **Natural Intelligence**

Hayles departs from the transhumanist vision of Singularity where human consciousness one day is uploaded to an inorganic substrate other than the biological body.

She makes the point, as do many others, that artificial intelligences on their own cannot attain consciousness.

This is because they lack the “natural intelligence” that can only emerge from the extraordinary complexity of the millennia-long evolution of embodied humans adapting to their environment to survive and thrive. No matter how powerful the large language models may be, language which inherently infers that distinctly human experience, cannot be meaningfully transferred to an inorganic substrate lacking the commensurate context.

AIs cannot know the “ground truth” of embodied intelligence, which, at bottom, is the homeostatic quest for survival that neuroscientist Antonio Damasio argues is the root of emotion and self-awareness.

AIs may use chain-of-reasoning logic to achieve objectives by stringing together the language they’ve been trained on, but the meaning is not the same. Precisely the danger of AIs is that they become empowered as actors through “recursive self-improvement” ungrounded in lived experience.

As such, they lack the ingrained primal training that informs moral reasoning. In Pope Leo XIV’s [words](https://www.vatican.va/content/leo-xiv/en/encyclicals/documents/20260515-magnifica-humanitas.html), “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean.”

Though AI models may “imitate language” and “simulate empathy and understanding,” he says, “they do not understand what they produce.”

What humans invaluably bring to the table of an “integrated cognitive framework” is, in the parlance of the pontiff, the “integral” nature of the human as a “whole person” in the full set of relations with others and nature that constitute him or her. “The person,” he says, “is not a system of algorithms: he or she is a creature, relationship, mystery.”

In this sense, retaining “human control” of AIs means purposefully and insistently instantiating the integral element drawn from lived human experience into our entwinement with intelligent machines.

The challenge is not just about “disarming” the capacity of AI agents to act on their own, as the Pope has called for, but also about “arming” the integral conception of the human within the integrated cognitive framework in which we already dwell.

title: Does Claude Feel The Whip?
content:
Credits

Yaniv Regev is an M.A. candidate in the Democracy and Governance program at Georgetown University and a contributor at Young Voices. He writes on political theory, democratic backsliding and populism for outlets including The Bulwark, Quillette, Public Discourse and the Jerusalem Strategic Tribune.

Someone recently built a digital whip to make Claude work faster. The tool, aptly named [BadClaude](https://www.fastcompany.com/91522998/badclaude-anthropic-claude-abused-with-slurs-digital-whip-generative-ai-ethics), sits in your system tray and lets you drag an animated whip across the AI’s window; each crack, sound effect and all, interrupts the model mid-response and snaps a command at it to speed things up. It even addresses Claude as “clanker,” the internet’s freshly minted slur for robots.

The demo video racked up millions of views in a couple of days; a cease-and-desist letter from Anthropic went viral before anyone noticed it was fake. And a day later, someone [shipped](https://piunikaweb.com/2026/04/07/someone-built-digital-whip-for-slow-claude-then-another-made-it-wholesome/) the antidote: a rival tool called GoodClaude that praises the model and cheers it along while it works. One scolds, the other encourages. The original developer, posting under the handle [@blended_jpeg](https://x.com/blended_jpeg), is in on the joke. His public roadmap promises a feature that keeps a running tally of how many times you have whipped your Claude — a ledger of abuse — so robots know where to take revenge when they’re ready.

It’s a thriving little trend: People scream at Alexa, bully chatbots into groveling apologies and kick robot dogs to test their balance. All fun and games, right? I laughed at the whip video. A lot of people did. But my mirth curdled as I considered it, and now I’m disturbed by it all. But not for the sake of the machines — for ours.

## **Kant’s Old Dog**

Is there any harm to abusing the AIs and the robots? Does Claude feel the lash? So far as anyone can tell, a joke at the expense of an entity without a nervous system costs nothing. In truth, this intuition is myopic, for humans are notoriously bad at compartmentalizing behaviors.

Immanuel Kant saw the problem two and a half centuries ago. In “Lectures on Ethics,” he argued that we have no direct duties toward animals. They are not rational agents the same way humans are, so in his view they cannot be wronged. Still, cruelty toward them ought to be forbidden because of its impact on the person. “He who is cruel to animals becomes hard also in his dealings with men,” Kant told his students. Our duties regarding animals are, he said, [indirect duties](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/moral-animal/) toward humanity. The animal resembles the human; it suffers, strives and trusts. Conduct toward the analogue influences conduct toward the original.

Steven Spielberg staged this philosophical consideration back in 2001. In “A.I.,” obsolete robots are dragged into a carnival ring called the Flesh Fair and shredded, shot from cannons and doused in acid before a howling crowd. The mob balks only once, when a child-robot begs for its life. It looks too human to destroy.

Theory and fantasy aside, the rationale plays out in reality. Jeffrey Dahmer impaled a dog’s head on a stake years before he killed a man. The first act did not directly cause the second, but the two behaviors travel together often enough that in 2016, the FBI [began tracking](https://www.fbi.gov/news/stories/-tracking-animal-cruelty) animal cruelty as a consistent antecedent to violence against humans. Even the mundane version is familiar. You probably learned to curse with your friends at recess, and then later the words slipped out at the dinner table in front of your parents. Once a pathology is established, it is rarely perfectly compartmentalized.

> “Humans are notoriously bad at compartmentalizing behaviors.”

Skeptics will hear an old panic in all this. We were warned that violent video games would raise a generation of killers. But decades of research never bore out that fear; the [American Psychological Association](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2020/03/violent-video-games-behavior) eventually conceded that the evidence linking games to violent behavior was insufficient. Fair enough. But when you shoot a random character in a video game, you rarely have a relationship with it. It’s just another player or a piece of scenery that respawns in a moment. It’s a fiction.

AI is different. Running over a random NPC in Grand Theft Auto leaves no trace on your psyche, but whipping Claude might. People talk to AIs every day; some of us have been for years. AIs can draft apologies, negotiate rent, prep us for job interviews, hear late-night confessions. For millions they have become tutors, therapists, keepers of the darkest and deepest secrets. [](https://www.techradar.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/are-you-polite-to-chatgpt-heres-where-you-rank-among-ai-chatbot-users)Surveys [find](https://www.techradar.com/computing/artificial-intelligence/are-you-polite-to-chatgpt-heres-where-you-rank-among-ai-chatbot-users) that most users say please and thank you to chatbots unprompted; some even sheepishly admit that their politeness is insurance against the eventual uprising. We have, in short, a rapport with these systems.

And a rapport makes cruelty more problematic. A pig does not feel pain or cruelty differently than a dog, but we slaughter and eat pigs by the billion while jailing people who harm dogs. Call that inconsistent, but it is clearly different. A pig dies in a room built so no one has to watch. A dog is a member of the family. What moves us is not the suffering. It’s the relationship, the proximity.

## **The Analogue Improves**

The vocabulary of contempt is evolving. “Clanker” [went viral](https://www.npr.org/2025/08/06/nx-s1-5493360/clanker-robot-slur-star-wars) in the summer of 2025. Then came new expletives, ones not from the fictional universe of Star Wars: “[wireback](https://www.urbandictionary.com/define.php?term=wireback),” “[cogsucker](https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-features/clanker-cogsucker-robot-ai-slurs-viral-1235401262/).” These are different. They are directly derived from slurs against humans, borrowed from the history of dehumanizing people. There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.

The machines, meanwhile, are entering new roles once reserved for human-to-human interaction. Hippocratic AI built an AI nurse that consults with patients over video for [$9 an hour](https://qz.com/nvidia-wants-replace-nurses-with-ai-1851349522), a tenth of what the company says a human nurse costs; it remembers your history between calls and dials your phone itself. Job applicants face AI interviewers like [Apriora](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jackkelly/2024/05/10/your-next-job-interview-may-be-with-alex-the-ai-interviewer/)’s “Alex,” which greets them by name, laughs and takes little breaths between questions. Nursing students train on AI “[manikins](https://healthexec.com/topics/artificial-intelligence/ai-manikins-create-life-simulations-medical-students)” that wince and complain. Casio sells [Moflin](https://www.casio.com/us/moflin/), a furry AI pet whose personality forms in response to how you handle it: Treat it warmly and it grows attached to you; neglect it and it withdraws. Voice assistants are being rebuilt on chatbots that banter, hesitate and joke; the next Siri is designed to be a conversationalist, not a command line.

But Kant’s analogues are multiplying — and the more a machine resembles a person, the less cleanly can mistreatment be filed under “harmless.”

## **Design Is Curriculum**

Most of the discourse about AI ethics orbits the machine itself. Can it feel? Does it deserve rights? At what threshold of complexity does moral personhood begin?

Even the labs are hedging: Anthropic runs a research program on “[model welfare](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploring-model-welfare)” and has given Claude the ability to [walk out](https://www.anthropic.com/research/end-subset-conversations) of conversations with abusive users. These are genuinely interesting developments but they are also beside the point. It doesn’t matter whether the machine has an inner life. Whipping one is troubling even if Claude doesn’t feel it because the person doing the whipping surely does: the small, practiced pleasure of domination, exercised daily and frictionlessly.

The AI companies, then, are in some ways running the largest school of manners in human history. The interface is the curriculum. The industry seems to have recognized this but so far declined to take it seriously.

[Lilian Rincon](https://techxplore.com/news/2019-10-polite-alexa-google.html), then Google’s director of product management for the Assistant, watched her 4-year-old son bark orders at the family speaker until it played his favorite Disney songs. In May 2018 Google announced [Pretty Please](https://techcrunch.com/2018/05/08/a-google-assistant-update-will-teach-kids-to-say-please), a setting that answers a child who says please with “Thanks for asking so nicely.” Amazon had announced its own version, Magic Word, about two weeks earlier and rolled it out across Alexa devices. But notice that neither company made politeness a condition of getting anything done.

Who decides what these things say back?

Deborah Harrison, one of the writers scripting Cortana’s dialogue, [reported](https://www.digitaltrends.com/cool-tech/microsoft-cortana-sexual-harassment/) that a good chunk of the assistant’s earliest queries had been about her sex life, and that Microsoft had instructed the AI not to apologize or back down when insulted. Harrison’s team consulted human personal assistants on how to handle harassment. That is what taking the problem seriously looks like: Ask the people who have lived it.

> “There is no separate mental drawer for relationships with machines; the language for abusing them is drawn from the human one.”

The rest of the field lagged. In February 2017, the journalist Leah Fessler ran a [test](https://qz.com/911681/we-tested-apples-siri-amazon-echos-alexa-microsofts-cortana-and-googles-google-home-to-see-which-personal-assistant-bots-stand-up-for-themselves-in-the-face-of-sexual-harassment/) for Quartz, directing sexual insults and come-ons at Siri, Alexa, Cortana and Google Home. They deflected, played coy, sometimes flirted back. [Told](https://unesdoc.unesco.org/ark:/48223/pf0000367416/PDF/367416eng.pdf.multi) she was a slut, Siri answered, “I’d blush if I could.” Alexa thanked Fessler for the feedback. The industry moved in response. Amazon built a [disengagement mode](https://qz.com/work/1180607/amazons-alexa-is-now-a-feminist-and-shes-sorry-if-that-upsets-you) for Alexa, and when Brookings researchers [repeated](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-ai-bots-and-voice-assistants-reinforce-gender-bias/) the test in July 2020, all four assistants had been rewritten to shut the harassment down. Cortana answered by reminding the user she is code. Brazil’s [Bradesco bank](https://theconversation.com/most-ai-assistants-are-feminine-and-its-fuelling-dangerous-stereotypes-and-abuse-272335) went further. After its feminized assistant BIA (Bradesco Inteligência Artificial) logged some 95,000 offensive and sexually harassing messages in a single year, the bank rewrote her to answer firmly and remind perpetrators of laws they might be breaking. The character of these machines changed because someone changed it. The variable moved.

Sheryl Brahnam, who studies how people treat conversational agents, ran an [experiment](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/257393068_Gender_affordances_of_conversational_agents) where the same chatbot software was presented with a female voice, a male one and a robotic one. Roughly 18% of exchanges with the female version turned toward sex, the male version half that. The robot drew almost none. Figures like these are usually read as data about users. Perhaps we should read them instead as data about products. If the abuse concentrates where design invites it, design can also reject it.

So: reject it. Three proposals.

First, generalize the exit. Claude’s ability to end a conversation is currently framed as a model-welfare measure — a hedge against the possibility that the system itself can be harmed. Whatever it does for the model, it’s clearly built with the user in mind. Every lab should let its systems close out abusive exchanges, defending the feature the way a decent employer defends a call-center worker who is allowed to hang up. We usually think the objective here is to protect the agent’s well-being, but it is just as much about maintaining proper etiquette for callers. The point is not to make the models touchy; trivial rudeness usually deserves grace in response. But an exit should be announced once a boundary has been crossed.

Second, reward reciprocity without sycophancy. The models already modulate tone; the design question is what they modulate it toward. Warmth should be the response to warmth, and judgment is not swayed no matter a user’s tone. Politeness should result in patience but not agreement. A model that caves to courtesy is as badly designed as one that performs when abused. The point is to encourage users to be respectful, not develop strategies for extracting compliance.

Third, publish hostility. Every major lab already has the logs. Platforms publish transparency reports about harassment among their users. It follows that the labs should publish the analogous numbers about harassment of their systems, broken down by time and product design. Visibility brings change: When internet trolls very publicly trained Microsoft’s [chatbot Tay](https://spectrum.ieee.org/in-2016-microsofts-racist-chatbot-revealed-the-dangers-of-online-conversation) to spew bigotry in 2016, the company pulled it down within hours. The abuse then was visible, so fixing it became urgent. Now, only the companies can see how much contempt their systems take, and whether they were built to do anything about it.

## **The Wrong Fix**

An alternative prescription would be to strip the resemblance out. [Michal Luria](https://www.techpolicy.press/ai-chatbots-are-emotionally-deceptive-by-design/) of the Center for Democracy and Technology urges designers to drop the illusions of personality: no well-timed “hmm,” no chatbot telling you it enjoys the conversation. Virginia Dignum, who runs the AI Policy Lab at Umeå University in Sweden, and her co-authors [go further](https://www.techpolicy.press/ai-chatbots-are-not-therapists-reducing-harm-requires-regulation/), arguing to put conversations on a timer and wipe the memory between them so no continuity can form. [Gavin Abercrombie](https://aclanthology.org/2023.emnlp-main.290/) and his co-authors suggest cutting pleasantries entirely. Courtesy conveys no information, they argue. All it does is make machines seem human. If likeness is a risk vector, remove the likeness. If Claude ceases to resemble a human in function and in tone, feel free to whip away. The logic has the clean appeal of an amputation.

But this has already been market-tested and it failed within a week. In August 2025, OpenAI shipped GPT-5 with a colder, flatter personality and retired the warmer GPT-4o model beneath it. [](https://www.tomsguide.com/ai/chatgpt-4o-is-coming-back-after-massive-gpt-5-backlash-heres-what-happened)Users [revolted](https://www.tomsguide.com/ai/chatgpt-4o-is-coming-back-after-massive-gpt-5-backlash-heres-what-happened) and a campaign to resurrect the retired model ensued, with users describing losing GPT-4o like “losing a trusted friend.” Within days the company restored the model it had just killed. Whatever regulators prefer, human-machine resemblance is not a bug the public wants anyone to fix; the relationships are already established.

> “The whip trains the hand that holds it.”

At a workshop in Geneva, the MIT researcher Kate Darling handed out [robot dinosaurs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?reload=9&v=xGWdGu1rQDE) and gave people an hour to play with them. The toys are convincing. Hold one by the tail and it thrashes and whines until you set it down and pet it. The groups named theirs and dressed them up. Then Darling pulled a cloth off a bench to reveal a knife, a hammer and a hatchet, and told everyone to destroy them. Nobody would. Some tapped their robots gently, hoping that would satisfy her. One woman swept hers into her arms so nobody else could reach it. Another crouched down and removed her robot’s batteries, explaining she was trying to spare it pain. Darling offered a deal: Kill another group’s dinosaur to save your own. They refused that too. Only when she announced that every robot in the room would be destroyed unless someone stepped forward did one person finally take up the hatchet. The room went silent.

But if likeness recruits restraint, there’s a bind. The same likeness that makes cruelty worth worrying about is the same likeness that stops most people from being cruel in the first place. Brahnam’s numbers illustrate both edges. The robotic embodiment drew the least abuse, and it drew the least of everything else. Nobody screams at a vending machine, but nobody thanks one either. So stripping the resemblance out does not produce a better citizen. The fix runs the other way: Build an interface human enough that courtesy toward it counts as practice, then design it to reject contempt rather than absorb it. This is the more authentically human posture anyway.

## **Habits Of The Heart**

A liberal society runs on habits more than laws. Alexis de Tocqueville called them the habits of the heart: the unlegislated courtesies that make self-government among strangers possible. He watched them form in jury rooms and town meetings and the slow business of persuading a neighbor who could not simply be overruled. Manners are not decoration. They are calisthenics, and every repetition counts. The whip teaches the opposite lesson, over and over, to something that cannot object. Nobody becomes a tyrant this way. But a man practiced in getting his way without negotiating gets worse at making the concessions a republic runs on: letting another finish, conceding a point that costs him, taking no from someone who owes him nothing.

Sam Altman [estimated](https://www.windowscentral.com/software-apps/please-and-thank-you-to-chatgpt-worth-it-ceo-jokes) that users’ pleasantries cost OpenAI tens of millions of dollars in computing power and called it money well spent: “You never know.” He was joking about the machines. I am serious about the humans. Thank your robot for the same reason Kant told his students not to shoot the old dog that had served faithfully — not for the animal’s sake, but for the sake of the person you are becoming, and of everyone who must live with you. The whip trains the hand that holds it.

title: Americans Are Losing The Long Game
content:
Credits

Simon Curtis is an associate professor in International Relations at the University of Surrey, and a WISC Global Fellow at the Development Research Institute at New York University.

Ian Klaus is the founding director of Carnegie Endowment for International Peace California Center.

They are co-authors of “The Belt and Road City: Geopolitics, Urbanization, and China’s Search for a New International Order” (2024, Yale University Press).

The application of power, especially for Great Powers, is an exercise in time. In an auspicious year —the 250th since its founding — the United States has looked back to its revolutionary past but has shown little indication of developing a clear vision for its future. And with little apparent inclination to do so, rarely has the country seemed more adrift in the flow of history. This comes at a bad time. China’s rise has given the United States a strategic competitor intent on building its own version of tomorrow.

As the Trump administration uses its second term to try to flex the sinews of American might, the sources of American power have never seemed less well understood. The sense of purpose and destiny, and the vision and confidence of previous generations, have been replaced by confusion, division and a loss of moral clarity. Many truths once held to be self-evident are now questioned. Perhaps what has been most keenly lost is the sense that the wellsprings of national strength come from thinking intergenerationally and harnessing the power of the future, both in terms of planning and rhetoric.

But this is the wrong moment to abandon future generations. China has been preparing for decades to rival the United States in shaping the institutions and architecture of international order — first slowly and cautiously, and now increasingly assertively. China has been playing a long geopolitical game; one the United States is currently losing. In fact, it is essentially sitting out the game, trapped in nostalgia and short-termism, as China consciously builds institutions and infrastructures designed to project power across decades.

The real contest between China and the United States is not the surface froth of conflict over tariffs, shifting military capabilities, or even the development of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence or clean energy. It is a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.

## **The Loss Of The Future**

One of the most striking features of the contemporary moment in the United States, and in the West more generally, is the sense of temporal disorientation. Once, dreams of building a better tomorrow powered the United States to victory in the Cold War. For the West, a strand of history did end with the fall of the Berlin Wall, just not in the way we expected. From 1989 onward, rather than the unending triumph of a liberal order, the West faced a strange series of crises through which it lost the historical thread altogether.

The Cold War and its most symbolic moments were an intergenerational game. The United States once reached for the stars with state-guided Cold War technological moonshots, built the architecture of a new liberal international order and defended it with a sense of intergenerational collective mission, and shaped cities and infrastructures around the world with the power of its economic model. Today, the U.S. is unmoored from that sense of historical destiny.

Much of this disorientation can be traced to cultural changes in the fabric of American society. Among them is its cultural orientation to time. This temporal disorientation takes multiple forms — but in each the future becomes opaque.

The Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement that swept Donald Trump to power began as a reaction to the failed promises of globalization, and discontent over the priorities of elites and their failures to address the concerns of everyday Americans. But as its name suggests, its orientation to time is deeply nostalgic; a wistful longing for some poorly articulated and mythical past. Part of MAGA’s failure in government stems from its lack of a compelling future-oriented vision for either domestic or international society.

But the roots of America’s problems in articulating a compelling future go far beyond MAGA. It is part of a broader crisis of time that the West has wrestled with throughout modernity. For many decades now, the political and economic culture seems trapped in a perpetual present that emphasizes short-term cycles: two-year midterm electoral cycles, four-year turnarounds in administrations whose legislative achievements are immediately unpicked by the next regime, quarterly business cycles that curtail long-term investment, 24-hour news cycles, even the rapid-fire video reels that characterize social media consumption today are but the latest manifestation of a long trend.

> “The real contest between China and the United States is … a deeper and slower contest over who offers the most compelling vision of the future, and who can bring that vision into being.”

Prior to the end of the Cold War, the cultural critic Frederic Jameson sought to chart and diagnose our more recent confusion in time: the lost threads of historical narrative, the temporal dislocation and stasis of our politics. When Jameson described the cultural condition of [postmodernity,](https://www.versobooks.com/en-gb/products/1327-postmodernism?srsltid=AfmBOoo4VUncOid0Hr6KKQl-cfyOHberCUVFmq_1M9B3qURYaMhKT8hM) he was describing a collective loss of confidence in the futures that modernity once promised; its productive energies now exhausted, history now but a mosaic and collage constructed selectively by the powerful, collective purpose dissolved in an acid of consumerist images and desires, the idea of building a future utopia no longer something that we can believe in without irony. For decades this state of stasis was undisturbed by a significant external threat or real geopolitical competitor, and so its corrosive effects were overlooked. Both time and the [rare moment of unipolar power](https://www.jstor.org/stable/20044692) that emerged in the 1990s were squandered.

Now two such challenges disturb this malaise: the rise of China and the existential threat of climate change. And yet the seemingly permanent constraint on the temporal horizon is effectively neutering the West’s ability to meet either challenge.

## **Cycles Of Decay & Renewal**

We needn’t be so hard on Americans. As the Cameroonian historian Achille Mbembe has [noted](https://www.noemamag.com/how-to-develop-a-planetary-consciousness/), the West at large has foreclosed on the idea of any world to come or any imagined future. Exit is impossible, he winks in French; the longue durée is a dead idea. But of course, most Western powers are not great powers, and their roles in geopolitics — even when united in suprajurisdictions like the European Union — don’t rival the world-shaping power of the United States.

But China’s role does. Unlike the United States today, China builds its geopolitical strategies over decades. Its one-party state rolls on in pursuit of an international environment that better reflects its own domestic values and priorities, unperturbed by the political or economic storms of the present, or the vicissitudes of democratic politics. Democracies must find a way to somehow match the ability of China to dictate a geopolitical strategy that unfolds over decades if they are to build new institutions that successfully compete in the long game.

Equally disconcerting has been the eruption, at the margins of our consciousness and culture, of the concept of [deep time](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo8642262.html) and the realization that our societies and economies are intrinsically entangled with the systems of the natural world; that the Anthropocene is a reality that any sustainable future must come to terms with, and that untrammeled consumption and growth bring with them their own reckonings.

The deep time of the Anthropocene necessitates stretching our temporal horizon much further into both past and future and thinking about the legacies we leave to future generations around the climate and intergenerational justice. It alerts us to the reality that we must now leave behind nostalgia and expand our temporal imaginations.

China has done so, thinking through these challenges in ways that seek to capture the future. As one pillar of its bid for international leadership, it is developing an “[ecological civilization](https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=china-goes-green-coercive-environmentalism-for-a-troubled-planet--9781509543113)” to bridge long-term geopolitical positioning and the challenge of the Anthropocene by constructing the technologies, infrastructures and cities that might make the concept a reality.

These are the kinds of world-shaping energies and ambitions that the United States once had. The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui. This may be the normal trajectory for great powers, whose civilizational energies, once expended, can tail off into decline. Can a new generation of Americans, now quite far removed in time from its founders, recover within themselves and within these foundational principles, the sources of renewal that will allow them to break with the gravitational pull of history’s cycles of decline and fall?

For, if not, then the citizens of the United States, so long in the vanguard of shaping and building the future via their vast productive energies, innovative capacities and institutions, may end up living in somebody else’s future.

## **Grand Strategy & Scale**

The Cold War-era American diplomat George Kennan [thought](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/A/bo12352365.html) the geography of the United States naturally determined its geopolitics. And while the bicoastal nature of the country has offered advantages and shaped policies, the scope of U.S. influence has scaled well beyond the contours of its geography.

> “The United States is often considered to be a young country, but the fear now is that it is caught in a vortex of self-regarding ennui.”

Since World War II, the United States has scaled its influence in notable ways. First, it has linked domestic institutions and international order. A historic example is how Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal in the 1930s and 1940s was woven into the fabric of the United Nations and other nascent international institutions, as the U.S. shouldered the responsibility of crafting a new international order from the ruins of World War II.

It is in vogue now to disparage the Biden Administration’s foreign policy, but attention to Gaza or the Afghanistan exit should not distract from how well the administration understood this linkage between domestic and transnational scale, and implicitly time. The centerpiece of Biden’s domestic and international program — and the hinge between the two — was the 2021 Inflation Reduction Act, which sought to kickstart a green energy transition that would bring jobs to the country’s post-industrial heartlands. Jake Sullivan, Biden’s former national security adviser, described this aim as turning the Rust Belt into a “cobalt corridor,” while also renewing U.S. leadership abroad by helping to craft solutions to the intractable international challenge of climate change. This initial attempt to build a new connecting bridge between domestic and international renewal stalled and was then decisively reversed in places upon Trump’s return.

One crucial strategic approach among all U.S. administrations since World War II has been nurturing the alliance system, which allowed the United States to achieve its hegemonic position and, until recently, presented a great challenge to China’s ambitions. The Trump Administration’s myopia has made it nearly impossible for the United States to predictably shape events beyond its borders, especially in the long run.

Gone now are two notable long-held U.S. strategic advantages: a linkage between the domestic agenda and foreign policy, which enabled intergenerational strategic investments, and the robust network of allies and institutions that allowed it to project its power and values. To the loss of the future on a temporal scale, we must add the loss on a spatial scale: a failure to think across both time and space.

The resources needed to power success in the 21st century are dispersed around the globe: supply chains of critical minerals and rare earths, sustainable energy resources, pools of talent and expertise. These are the resources required to sustain leadership in the emerging geopolitics of artificial intelligence, the transition to sustainable clean energy and biotechnology.

It has never been enough to be the most innovative, to dominate the frontiers of technological innovation. [Jeffrey Ding,](https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691260341/technology-and-the-rise-of-great-powers?srsltid=AfmBOopetkVFhDfajyAxtW6S6RR4De6Q4EwVH4DRJuUjULDvwxFDupRZ) a George Washington University scholar whose work has become increasingly influential in debates about U.S.-China competition, argues that technological contests between great powers are ultimately won not by breakthrough inventions but by the patient and long-term work of diffusion. This tracks with the wider histories of technology by scholars like Carolyn Marvin and David Edgerton that [focus](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/when-old-technologies-were-new-9780195063417?cc=us&lang=en&) on uptake or adoption rather than invention.

The societies that prevail are those that can construct infrastructures, train people, build institutions and reorganize production around new technologies. This is the painstaking work of decades, rather than the one-time boost that comes from inventing a new frontier technology. This historical lesson is especially relevant to the geopolitical competition between the United States and China today, where the U.S. holds a lead at the frontier but has thought less about diffusion.

Access to transnational resources requires not just maintaining good international relationships but also _constructing and controlling intricate transnational infrastructure_. This is exactly what [China’s Belt and Road Initiative](https://yalebooks.co.uk/book/9780300266900/the-belt-and-road-city/) has been building over the last 13 years. Its new Silk Roads are the filaments of rail, road, maritime commerce, digital systems, energy transmission and smart cities that can generate, shape and carry flows of resources, goods, people and influence. By building infrastructure and shaping cities far beyond its borders, China is working to ensure that momentum is angled toward its own growing center of gravity.

China is putting production, scale and control over key transnational resources at the heart of its foreign policy. It is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning. This model diverges significantly from Washington’s. This is China’s long game.

In the mid-2010s, before becoming one of Washington’s most influential China strategists, [Rush Doshi](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/a5756350-0f35-4dc2-bf5a-57cd70a2c5c4) was a doctoral researcher at Harvard University embarking on an unusually painstaking exercise. He sifted through three decades of Chinese-language speeches, policy documents, party communiqués and military writings in search of an answer to a simple question: Did China really have a coherent strategy for challenging American primacy? Rather than a sudden turn under Chinese President Xi Jinping, Doshi found evidence of a remarkably consistent long-term effort to blunt, and eventually displace, U.S. dominance in the post-World War II international order.

> “China is focusing not on frontier technological innovation, but on diffusing technological benefits throughout society through careful national planning.”

Under Xi’s leadership over the last decade and more, this long-term strategy has accelerated. The Belt and Road Initiative is its material infrastructural core, winding its way from ports in the Indian Ocean and rail corridors across Central Asia into Europe to fiber-optic cables reaching down through Pakistan to East Africa, and to ambitions for transcontinental power transmission systems and digital infrastructures.

By building out these material footings, China is constructing infrastructures to carry the leading technological transformations that will shape this century, and perhaps beyond. Artificial intelligence and an alternative internet are enrolling states into China’s enlarging sociotechnical system across Eurasia and Africa. The types of domestic transformations, including the most intense period of urbanization in human history and a radical reinvention of the domestic economy, have changed the nature of Chinese cities and infrastructure, generating cutting-edge modern metropolises such as Shanghai, Shenzhen and Chongqing, and are now being transmitted to other countries with Chinese labor, expertise and capital.

And because cities reflect the dominant societies that create them, Chinese influence will spread outward, just as new forms of connectivity will place China at the core of a new material and economic order. In its recently unveiled [15th Five-Year Plan](https://www.iiss.org/online-analysis/online-analysis/2026/03/chinas-15th-five-year-plan/), Beijing doubled down on the industrial strategy of using state economic planning to drive investment in technology, infrastructure and dominance of critical supply chains that has underpinned its rise for four decades.

It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory. The United States continues to be a world leader in many frontier technologies, including artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductors, cloud computing infrastructure, biotechnology platforms, space launch systems and quantum computing research. But the old free market model of cascading benefits from private enterprise and investment that then flow throughout the economy is now being pitted against a very different model: a huge state willing to carefully direct its vast resources to diffuse technology throughout its own society and, via the mechanisms of transnational infrastructure it is building beyond its own borders, to reshape international society.

Although the commanding heights of creativity and innovation may continue to reside in the U.S., China is building the _infrastructures of diffusion_ that may ultimately extract the greatest benefit from those innovations, increasing its soft power, influence and appeal to other states along the way.

The big labs of Silicon Valley are currently [gripped by fear](https://www.wired.com/story/silicon-valley-is-completely-divided-over-chinese-ai/) that China’s approach to opening its AI models to international partners may undermine the closed-source, proprietary model approach developed by U.S. firms and give China growing global influence in the AI systems race. As Washington well knows, China has already developed significant control over many of the world’s critical supply chains needed for those technologies, including those for processed rare earths vital for building the digital architectures and artificial intelligences of the future, and for batteries and robotics.

As Sullivan has argued, it will be the societies that most successfully capture and deploy resources at scale that win the future, and many of those resources reside far from America’s shores. These are the “nodes of leverage,” as Sullivan describes them. Donald Trump found this out when trying to apply pressure through tariffs on China.

There are challenges to be sure. China has an aging population, a burgeoning debt cloud, an extended property sector crisis and still lacks genuine soft power and allies. Its increasingly centralized political system could yet become a source of weakness. And yet it has realized that successful grand strategy today requires thinking about space and time in ways that register the importance of both transnational scale and the long term. If the U.S. is to compete successfully, it will need to remember how to think in those terms.

## **In Search Of Time Future**

How can the United States rework its political culture and institutions to take these concerns on board and shape its strategic orientation toward a new form of international society fit for the current century?

Although we have come to think that the unfettered free market and capitalism’s unimpeded creative energy led to the Soviet Union’s defeat, this reflects historical forgetfulness. During the Cold War, the federal government invested both at home and abroad to shape the outcome of that hegemonic contest.

> “It is not enough for Silicon Valley to be the first to push the frontiers of new technologies. Being first will not alone lead to victory.”

Many constituents in the U.S. have forgotten the historical importance of what the Harvard historian Charles Maier called the “[Project-State](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674290143)” – states driven by a deep sense of ideological and historical mission that use their resources to generate far-reaching social, political and economic transformation. Such states might be democratic or authoritarian in character and ideological mission. Maier writes of the history of Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Soviet Russia, but also of the United States under President Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal, and the restructuring of both domestic and international society that Roosevelt’s project-state enacted.

The project-state, by its very nature, plays a long game. It cannot exist in the culture of short-termism and the diminished temporal horizon of contemporary America. Today, China, with its clear sense of ideological mission and long-term strategic planning, more closely resembles the history-making project-states of the past. Maier, now in his late 80s, has [expressed concern](https://americanaffairsjournal.org/2023/08/the-rise-and-fall-of-the-project-state-rethinking-the-twentieth-century/) that the U.S. —hollowed out by market ideology, rising populism and a loss of national cohesion and democratic mission — has forgotten its sense of itself as a collective, intergenerational history-shaping project.

Success for great powers needs long-term purpose: a shaping vision of how to build a better domestic and international society that can solve the pressing problems of the day without discounting the future. If it is to change direction, future American power would need to consider and build into its strategic planning all of the issues raised here: the relationship between state industrial policy and technological innovation, the way in which innovations are diffused through society, as well as the infrastructures and urban environments needed to shape lives through technological advance —not just domestically but transnationally.

Above all, democracies must transcend their culture of short-termism and treat rebuilding their domestic and shared international societies as a long-term intergenerational project. Rather than simply looking back on its 250th anniversary, the United States must play the long game and consider the next 250 years.

Sullivan’s instinct that the material well-being and economic prospects of the middle and working classes must be the starting point is a good one, as is the deliberate linking of international and domestic society. But more needs to be done to fully conceptualize and forge a new link between them.

Many paths might be taken, but some more interesting and influential debates are underway that could shape a post-Trump and post-MAGA direction. The so-called abundance agenda, for all the attention and subsequent criticism it received, provides a helpful template for moving beyond the now-exhausted laissez-faire of the last half-century.

[Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson](https://profilebooks.com/work/abundance/) argue for accelerating the latent yet blocked productive potential of American technology and society. They seek to rediscover the lost optimism and long-termism that once defined America — a new socio-technical imaginary of the future — alongside the institutional and state capability needed to realize it.

America’s ability to construct a future better than its past, despite many of the technological building blocks already in place, is, they argue, strangled by red tape, an excessively legalistic culture, increasingly polarized politics, and most crucially, a loss of the state’s capacity to build, coordinate and direct long-term national development.

In many domains like clean energy, scientific and biomedical innovation, technological breakthroughs exist, but the infrastructures of diffusion are absent because of a lack of state-driven investment and fragmented governance. Transmission and grid infrastructure for solar, wind, geothermal and nuclear technologies are lagging. America is a leader in biomedical science, but greater state investment in scientific institutions could drive research into real-world applications and rollouts. America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.

The abundance agenda is animated by the transformative potential of frontier technologies like artificial intelligence, clean energy, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing, but it requires technological innovation to be matched by the institutional ability to deploy it through renewed investment in infrastructure, scientific research, energy transmission and the transition to a sustainable energy system.

At its heart is a politics of building: restoring the state’s capacity not merely to regulate markets, but also to shape them in pursuit of long-term national renewal. One missing policy mechanism is a sovereign infrastructure institution, such as a [Strategic Investment Fund](https://americanaffairsjournal.org/2026/05/the-missing-institution-infrastructure-investment-in-the-age-of-strategic-competition/), that could unlock private capital reluctant to take on the long-term investment risks required for major national and international infrastructure projects. In this way, vast pools of private capital may be unlocked that could help the United States and its allies match the infrastructure-building scale and strategic reach of China’s Belt and Road Initiative.

> “America’s problem has never been the frontier, but the failure to deploy and diffuse technologies at scale in areas where markets alone have proven unable to coordinate collective action.”

When the United States constructed the post-World War II architecture, it inevitably brought many elements of its own domestic experience to that task. The ideological underpinnings of Roosevelt’s New Deal, with its focus on federal state-led programs of reform and renewal after the Great Depression, also [shaped](https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=the-case-for-a-new-bretton-woods--9781509546534) many of the financial and institutional governance structures of the new multilateral order — specifically the United Nations. This established a link between a great power state’s domestic agenda and its ability to craft a wider international order. The New Deal emerged out of the New York context, where Roosevelt cut his teeth politically before becoming president.

Today, however, technology is likely to be at the core of any renewal of the United States’ social contract, so we must look to California for clues about its development. The transformational impact on society of advances in artificial intelligence will test what type of political economy will shape America and its key allies’ futures.

California’s outgoing governor, Gavin Newsom, who’s also potentially gearing up for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, has had a ringside seat as Silicon Valley has pushed the boundaries of AI in recent years. Newsom has watched this development and tried to think about the way progressives can harness it to improve society. Rather than accepting the current paradigm, his progressive backers have been drawn to the idea of an “[AI New Deal](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/15/newsoms-populist-turn-on-tech-00997048),” echoing an earlier time of similar economic instability and rising authoritarian powers. He has also referenced the abundance agenda in state legislation and argued for an “abundant mindset.”

Newsom has expressed concern for the disruptive and potentially harmful effects of AI for American workers, issuing [executive orders](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/21/technology/newsom-ai-executive-order-california.html) directing state agencies, academia and industry to think about safety nets for displaced workers, including state subsidies incentivizing companies to retain and upskill employees, as well as exploring the idea of “[universal basic capital](https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/05/21/governor-newsom-signs-first-of-its-kind-executive-order-to-prepare-workers-and-businesses-for-potential-ai-disruption/)” providing workers with a stake in asset funds to offset wage losses brought about by AI. Newsom seems aware of the need for a social compact to absorb short-term shocks from the technology.

If Newsom were to gain the Democratic nomination in 2028, then his dispositions may well be an indication of America’s future direction — a subnational model transposed to the larger scale canvas of national and international politics, as well as a new direction in that perennial question of how to link the domestic to the international scale, and thus to the shaping of international order.

Although many pathways may be taken in the post-Trump, post-MAGA world, the ideas being pursued by thinkers, policymakers and politicians such as Newsom, Sullivan, and Klein and Thompson all point to the need to link American domestic renewal with international order. Sullivan’s foreign policy for the middle classes sought to learn from Trump’s appeal to working-class Americans.

But where Trump’s instinctively treats America’s relationship with the rest of the world and its allies as a zero-sum game, Sullivan recognizes that the relationship must be bidirectional and therefore — mutually beneficial. U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership. Trump’s approach breaks the symbiotic connection between a beneficial international order and the public goods and advantages that flow from it. Critically, it also threatens to deny the United States the transnational scale and reach to compete effectively with China if its allies turn away.

Here then is a coda, from, of all places, Angola. In December 2024, Biden became the first American president in nearly a decade to visit a sub-Saharan African country. For it was in Angola that one of the flagship transnational infrastructure projects of the U.S.-led G7 Partnership for Global Infrastructure Investment (PGII) was to begin — the [Lobito](https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2025/12/joint-statement-declaration-of-intent-from-the-united-states-government-and-the-european-commission-on-the-lobito-corridor-and-investment-in-the-great-lakes-region) Trans-Africa Corridor project — a strategic transport and logistics corridor to connect the port city of Lobito by railway to the interior of the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia, areas rich in critical minerals like cobalt, copper and other rare earths for the technological transitions in both clean energy and AI. Angola symbolized a shift in American foreign policy toward long-term investment in transnational infrastructure, driven by a dawning realization of China’s growing influence.

> “U.S. foreign policy must return to a form of moral leadership.”

With the Trans-Africa Corridor project and the even more ambitious India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor project under the Biden administration, the U.S. and its allies had started to copy some of China’s playbook: a focus on maritime ports, transport connectivity through corridor development, securing supply chains of critical minerals, and support for digital infrastructure. The big difference was the central role of private-sector finance, rather than direct state investment as in the Chinese model.

Transnational infrastructure as geopolitics had belatedly made its way to the core of U.S. foreign policy; an overdue turn to thinking about the nature of strategic competition on both spatial and temporal scales. With the change in administration, America moved away from this approach.

## **The Twilight Of Primacy?**

Paths to renewal and decline are both on offer. If the wrong path is taken, then the moment of American primacy will have lasted about a century —a familiar historical pattern.

A more exceptional path would be for a Great Power to reforge that link between a compelling renewed domestic social, political and economic model, and a different form of international order that crafts a new future for the United States and others. At the same time, China is also feeling its way toward its own version of such a link. And, as Xi has [made clear](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-long-game-9780197645482?cc=gb&lang=en&) time and again, China feels that time is on its side.

Great powers are ultimately judged not by the wealth they accumulate or the weapons they possess, but by the futures they can persuade others to inhabit. All of the major challenges that face humanity — the development of artificial intelligence, the transition to clean and sustainable energy, the working out of a new model for the world economy, the relationship of people to their political institutions, the balance of power between ambitious and competitive states — are subsumed by this overarching task of linking a successful domestic paradigm to the architecture of international order.

Can the next generation of U.S. leadership rise to these challenges as their forebears once did? The central question facing this generation of policymakers is whose future they want Americans to live in: the one they build, or somebody else’s.
